content:
[Product Question] My wife uses an expensive instant facelift serum. It tightens the skin under her eyes to remove wrinkles, and she loves it, but I'd like to find a cheaper alternative. Any suggestions?
I understand this may not be quite the focus for this sub, but so far, this is the best sub I've found so far that is willing to discuss this, so I hope you'll indulge me on this.

My wife is elderly, but has great skin.  The one she buys is called "Epilift", and it's $100 for 30 ml ($100/oz). She applies it and it does the trick in about 3 minutes, but I'm sure there must be other products that do the same or better for much less.   Also note that she's mainly interested in the short term firming effects of this product.  

#Question: Are there other products you would recommend that do the same thing as Epilift (instant anti-wrinkle)?  And perhaps less expensive?  Or perhaps recommend another resource or subreddits that would help.

###Ingredients of Epilift Serum:

**Purified Water**    

**Sodium Silicate** - Adhesive/glue, also called "Water Glass".  This is likely the primary "active" ingredient.  For example, see [this patent](https://www.google.com/patents/US20170189299) by L'oreal that talks about sodium silicate.

**Magnesium Aluminum Silicate** - Thickener.  Derived from refined and purified clay that is used primarily as a thickener in cosmetics and beauty products. It is naturally of a flaky, white consistency and is used most often as a filler in deodorants, shaving creams and thick lotions

**Propylene Glycol**  - Used in a wide variety of applications ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propylene_glycol#Applications)). I think it's probably used as a humectant.  From Wikipedia [humectant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humectant): *In pharmaceuticals and cosmetics, humectants can be used in topical dosage forms to increase the solubility of a chemical compound's active ingredients, increasing the active ingredients' ability to penetrate skin, or its activity time. This hydrating property can also be needed to counteract a dehydrating active ingredient (e.g., soaps, corticoids, and some alcohols).*

**Sodium Carboxylmethycellulose**  -   Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) is a water-soluble anionic linear polymer. In food, pharmaceutical and cosmetic applications, highly purified types (99.5%+) are required and are referred to as cellulose gum.  [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboxymethyl_cellulose#Uses)

**Collagen**  - In food, collagen is used to make gelatin.  In cosmetic surgery, it used to be injected to plump up skin.  In a serum, it might be effective as a humectant, or just helpful for texture.  Here's a good article on it's use in skin care [link](https://intothegloss.com/2016/03/collagen-skin-care/).
 
**\* Palmitoyl Oligopeptide**  

**\* Hyaluronic Acid**  - A naturally occurring carbohydrate polymer. It's replaced collagen as an injectable in cosmetic surgery. In a serum, it's touted as useful since it holds a lot of water.  But if it's so dang good at holding water, does it really release that water to help hydrate skin?  

**\* Acetyl Hexapeptide-8** (Argireline aka ["Botox in a bottle"](http://bioregenerativesciences.com/argireline-botox-bottle/))  

**\* Palmitoyl Tetrapeptide-7**  

**Phenoxyethanol**  

**Ethylhexylglycerin**  

_____

**\* Newer version of product contains these additional ingredients.**

_____

**EDIT:**  Thanks everyone for helping out! It seems that the primary ingredient is the Sodium Silicate, so we'll be looking at products from reputable brands that contain this ingredient.  Also, it appears that L'oreal recently filed for a patent for a product containing this ingredient, so maybe they'll be coming out with a product that uses it.  (I have no relationship with them or any cosmetic company.)
